definition: AlexNet is a convolutional neural network architecture developed for image classification tasks, notably achieving prominence through its performance in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC).
details: It classifies images into 1,000 distinct object categories and is regarded as the first widely recognized application of deep convolutional networks in large-scale visual recognition. Developed in 2012 by Alex Krizhevsky in collaboration with Ilya Sutskever and his Ph.D. advisor Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto, the model contains 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons. The original paper's primary result was that the depth of the model was essential for its high performance, which was computationally expensive, but made feasible due to the utilization of graphics processing units (GPUs) during training. The three formed team SuperVision and submitted AlexNet in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge on September 30, 2012. The network achieved a top-5 error rate of 15.3% to win the contest, more than 10.8% points better than the runner-up. The architecture influenced a large number of subsequent work in deep learning, especially in applying neural networks to computer vision.

explainer.lead: AlexNet is an eight-layer neural network that learns to recognize objects in images, sorting them into 1,000 categories. Its decisive win in the 2012 ImageNet competition showed that deep networks trained on GPUs could outperform established computer-vision approaches and helped make learned image features the dominant approach.

tiers.eli5: AlexNet is like a team of inspectors passing a photograph along an assembly line. The first inspectors notice simple visual patterns, later ones combine those patterns into useful clues, and the final inspectors choose among 1,000 kinds of objects. Its big ImageNet win helped show that this learn-from-examples approach could work much better than many systems built around hand-designed clues.
tiers.practitioner: AlexNet takes 224×224 image crops and produces class probabilities, using five convolutional layers followed by three fully connected layers. The original training used 1.2 million ImageNet images, batches of 128, ReLU activations, dropout of 0.5, and two GTX 580 GPUs for five to six days; the network had to be split across the GPUs because it did not fit in one GPU's 3GB of VRAM. For prediction, it averages probabilities from five crops and their horizontal reflections, while its 2012 competition entry averaged predictions from seven trained networks.
tiers.paperLevel: AlexNet is a deep convolutional classifier with 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons, structured as (CONV → RN → MP)2 → (CONV3 → MP) → (FC → DO)2 → Linear → softmax, where CONV3 denotes three consecutive convolutional layers. It used ReLU activations, local response normalization, max-pooling, dropout with probability 0.5, and momentum gradient descent on 1.2 million training images for 90 epochs. Depth was central to its performance but computationally expensive: the original network required two GPUs because it exceeded the memory of one, and the competition result used an ensemble rather than a single network.

usedIn.detail: Classifies images into 1,000 object categories using features learned from training data.

usedIn.name: ImageNet competition systems
usedIn.detail: An ensemble of seven AlexNets won ILSVRC 2012 with a 15.3% top-5 error rate.

usedIn.name: Computer-vision research

components.name: Convolutional layers
components.detail: The first five layers learn visual features and use ReLU activation, with layers 3, 4, and 5 connected without intervening pooling or normalization.

components.name: Response normalization
components.detail: Local response normalization follows layers in the early convolutional stages.

components.name: Max-pooling layers
components.detail: Pooling follows selected convolutional stages and reduces the spatial representation passed onward.

components.name: Fully connected layers
components.detail: Three final layers combine the learned features, with ReLU on the first two and dropout during training.

components.name: Softmax output
components.detail: The final linear layer and softmax produce probabilities for the 1,000 object categories.

components.name: Two-GPU split
components.detail: Except for the last layer, the network was duplicated across two GPUs so that it could be trained within their memory limits.

flow: Scale an image so its shorter side is 256 pixels, then take 224×224 patches for the network.
Pass a patch through the convolutional, normalization, and pooling stages to build visual features.
Feed those features through the fully connected layers and softmax to obtain 1,000 category probabilities.
At test time, repeat prediction for five patches and their horizontal reflections.
Average the probabilities from all 10 patches to produce the final prediction.
explainer.origin: Alex Krizhevsky developed AlexNet in 2012 with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto. Competing as team SuperVision, they submitted it to ILSVRC on September 30, 2012, where it won with a 15.3% top-5 error rate, more than 10.8 percentage points ahead of the runner-up.
explainer.lineage: Its small-scale architectural predecessor was LeNet-5, with earlier CNN ideas including Fukushima's neocognitron and prior GPU-trained networks by Chellapilla, Raina, and Cireșan and collaborators. AlexNet replaced the prevailing emphasis on manually engineered features such as SIFT, SURF, and HoG with a prominent demonstration that features could be learned directly from large-scale image data, influencing much later deep-learning work in computer vision.
explainer.whyItMatters: AlexNet connected three ingredients—deep convolutional networks, the large ImageNet training set, and practical GPU computation—in a system whose competition margin was difficult to ignore. Its success helped turn learning features directly from data from a minority position into the dominant direction in computer vision.
